sections.heading: A single slit produces minima where two slits produce maxima

blocks.p: This is the part that trips people up: for a single slit of width $a$, the condition $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$ gives **dark** fringes, the opposite of the double-slit formula on [Young's Double Slit](/resources/wave-optics-youngs-double-slit), where the same-looking condition gives *bright* fringes. The reason: a single slit isn't two point sources interfering: it's infinitely many point sources across the slit width interfering with *each other*, and at these specific angles they cancel out in pairs.
The central band between the first minima on either side is the **central maximum**, far brighter and wider than any of the side bands.
Its full width on a screen a distance $D$ away is the gap between the two first minima:
The weaker secondary maxima sit roughly halfway between minima, at $a\sin\theta \approx \left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda$, and each is only half as wide as the central one.
Light of wavelength 600 nm passes through a slit 0.2 mm wide. Find the angle to the first minimum, and its position on a screen 1.5 m away.
For such a small angle, $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ in radians, and the position on screen is $y \approx D\sin\theta$:
The central maximum spans from $-4.5$ mm to $+4.5$ mm, so its width is $\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a} = 9$ mm.

A grating is many equally-spaced slits, spacing $d$ apart. Unlike a single slit, this produces sharp, bright **principal maxima**, the same form as the double-slit condition, just with far more slits reinforcing each other:
Since $\sin\theta$ can't exceed 1, the highest order you can see is the largest whole number $n$ with $n \leq \dfrac{d}{\lambda}$.
A grating has 5000 lines per centimetre. Find the angle of the first-order maximum for sodium light, $\lambda = 589\text{ nm}$, and the highest order visible.
**Solution:** The line spacing is the reciprocal of the line density:

For the highest order, $\dfrac{d}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2000}{589} \approx 3.4$, so orders up to $n = 3$ appear on each side of the centre. A 4th order would need $\sin\theta \approx 1.18$, which is impossible.

sections.heading: Single slit, double slit and grating compared

table.caption: The condition that looks the same means different things

list: **Treating $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$ as a bright fringe.** For a single slit it marks the dark fringes.
**Halving the central maximum.** Its width runs from the first minimum on one side to the first minimum on the other: $\dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}$, not $\dfrac{\lambda D}{a}$.
**Including $n = 0$ as a minimum.** At $\theta = 0$ every part of the slit is in phase, which is the brightest point of the pattern.
**Forgetting to convert lines per centimetre.** 5000 lines/cm means $d = 2\times10^{-4}$ cm, which has to be converted to the same unit as $\lambda$ before dividing.

exam.note: Single-slit diffraction and the width of the central maximum are part of Wave Optics in the JEE Main and NEET Physics syllabus, usually tested alongside Young's double slit. Diffraction gratings are covered in first-year engineering physics.

related.intro: The same wave rules apply to electrons, whose de Broglie wavelength is small enough for a crystal lattice to act as a grating.
